title: Where the chain breaks
hookLine: between feeling and craving there is a gap where the chain can be cut

lines: A HOT FLASH. THEN THE STORY.
cards: Someone cuts in front of you in line. There's a hot flash of unpleasantness, right in the chest. That part is quick and nobody chose it.
Then, in less than a blink, the second part arrives: the story, the glare, the rehearsed speech, the replay on the drive home. The two can blur into one event. They aren't one.
Between them there's a seam, and some teachers point to it as the place in the twelve links where the chain can be cut.

teach.b: Look at the middle of the chain. Contact gives rise to feeling: pleasant, painful or neither. Feeling gives rise to craving: want more, want it gone.
The suttas don't use the word gap; that image comes from how some teachers apply the links.
But the suttas do say a trained follower of the Buddha still feels. Still has a body, still meets heat and cold and rude people. What doesn't follow is the craving.
So the link from feeling to craving isn't welded. The Buddha pictured it in a sutta called the Arrow, in the Connected Discourses, a different arrow from Malunkyaputta's.
When an untrained person is touched by a painful feeling, he sorrows and laments and becomes distraught.
He feels two pains, one in the body and one in the mind, like a man shot with one arrow and then shot again with a second.

teach.h: THE FIRST ARROW AND THE SECOND.
teach.b: The trained person feels the first arrow and isn't hit by the second. The first arrow is feeling. The second is everything we pile on top.
That's the seam, and it's where practice works: not by refusing to feel, but by meeting the feeling cleanly, so craving has nothing to grab.
Now the week, from the top. Three turns: each truth known, its task known, its task done. A handful of leaves: only what helps.
Salla: treat the wound before asking who shot it. Kacchapa: a rare human life. Dependent arising in four lines.
Nidana, on the painted wheel. And today, the place to cut.

how: In several Buddhist meditation traditions, practitioners note feelings as pleasant, unpleasant or neutral as they arise, so that craving and aversion can be seen before they take hold.

o: an emotion like anger or joy
the craving that follows a feeling

games.q: match each piece to today's teaching.
p: the grief and story piled on

s: the suttas use the exact word gap for this point in the chain
the image comes from how teachers apply the links; the suttas show feeling without craving.
in the Arrow sutta, the trained person still feels bodily pain
he feels the first arrow and isn't hit by the second.
cutting the chain means refusing to feel anything
it means meeting the feeling cleanly, so craving has nothing to grab.

games.q: you stub your toe hard. by the Arrow sutta, what can training change?
o: the second arrow: the grief, story and anger on top.
games.why: the trained person still feels the first arrow, the bodily pain, but isn't struck by the second.

practice: Sit still and wait for something to happen: an itch, a sound, an ache, a pleasant warmth. The moment you notice it, label it softly, pleasant, unpleasant or neither; that's the first arrow.
Then watch with real curiosity for the next half-second, the lean toward or away, and if you see it, you've found the seam.

wordCard.voice: Vedana. The felt tone of an experience, pleasant, painful or neither, the link just before craving: the first arrow comes, and the second doesn't have to.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit vedanā: feeling, the felt tone of pleasant, painful or neither, the link just before craving.

carryVoice: Your line: cut between. Met cleanly, a feeling leaves craving nothing to grab. Three hundred fifty days now.

sources.ref: SN 12.1 (the twelve links: feeling conditions craving)
